newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil shrs end strongly higher after wild session.
newsitem.headline: Brazil shrs end strongly higher after wild session.

text.p: Brazilian shares closed strongly higher after seesawing wildly on reports, later denied, that the government's leader in Congress' lower house had resigned, brokers said.

A spokeswoman for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said Dep. Luis Eduardo Magalhaes agreed to stay on the job despite apparent anger over Communications Minister Sergio Motta's criticism of government-allied parties in Congress.
The Sao Paulo bolsa's Bovespa index ended 1.57 percent higher at 12,427 points, a rise of 192 points from Tuesday's close, on turnover of 1.421 billion reais.

The market rose more than three percent early in the day, only to erase the gains and fall by more than three percent minutes after news reports broke that Magalhaes planned to resign. It later bounced back just as quickly.
"Speculation on the news about Luis Eduardo Magalhaes dominated the market," one local trader said.
"The market is extremely nervous, very volatile. Any news will have an effect."

The bolsa's rise was led by an 8.6 percent increase in telecoms equipment firm Ericsson Telecomunicacoes, which ended at 65.70 reais, and federal power holding Eletrobras preferred, which rose 4.69 percent to close at 625 reais.

The news about Magalhaes caused the bolsa's benchmark share, Telebras preferred, to plunge to 147 reais from 161 reais in five minutes. It later rose again to close at 155.80 reais, a rise of 0.84 percent on the session. The market pared some gains at the end of the day, but closed strongly higher, although jittery after days of wild swings.
"I'm quite surprised at the strength of the market," said an equities analyst at a foreign investment bank in Sao Paulo.
With Wednesday's gains, Brazilian stocks moved closer to recouping its losses from last week, when the Bovespa dropped 15 percent on speculation and profit-taking on fears of a devaluation.
Brokers declined to speculate on Thursday's session, saying the market's current volatility was likely to continue making it next to impossible to predict a trend.
